source:
Specific place chosen because it's where John Kelly (1750-1809) was born. Year 1819 given as the 1819 edition of Manx bible has plural examples, and I have read that this dictionary was used for bible translations from the late 1700s onwards, even though it was published later.

The word rannag seems to be the most popular word for 'frog' among revivalists, but I was unable to find any attestations from native speakers. The earliest extant occurrence seems to be in Douglas Fargher's 1969 The Manx Have a Word for it Book 4 Insects, Reptiles etc. Fargher was known for rejecting foreign loans and calques, and creating his own phrases and words to replace them. In this text, he says The common frog [...] is rannag, but this word became lost during the course of time, suggesting that he had not heard any native speakers use it. He claims that the word was preserved in the place-name 'Poyll Ny Rannagyn' (pool of the frogs), but no other mention of this placename seems to be available in other texts.

It may well be that this seemingly Latin-derived name was used on the island long ago, but in the absence of any native attestation I have not included it as an entry on this map.

I couldn't track down the informant to confirm she was from the area or where she might have got her Gaelic from. It's hard to know what her forename would have been on records (it wouldn't necessarily be an anglicised Síghle). Twenty years later the LASID reports no native Irish can be found in any of Leinster. I don't know what the situation was in the 1930s, but Piatt's 1933 Gaelic Dialects of Leinster certainly treats it as all but dead, with the latest evidence of Maynooth having native speakers being from the late 1880s.

Hence it seems likely to me that the informant was either not a native speaker, or a native speaker of another area's Gaelic. I will update this note if I am able to find out more. I thought I would include this datapoint rather than automatically assume it does not represent any local dialect.

note:
In a riddle I have seen repeated many times around Galway and Mayo. The riddle included in this book is in a fuller form. The answer to the riddle elsewhere is always a word meaning frog. Here the answer is Athadán no frog air snamh. meaning 'athadán or frog swimming'. But I don't see how athadán could be some different creature that is an alternative answer. I'm sure it's an alternative name. Does it mean 'flighty thing' or 'eloper', from athadh + án? Or perhaps more likely, áth + adán (alternative form of án), with áth meaning shallow part of a river.

LASID point 35 gives a list of alternative words for frog heard in different areas. [ɑːdɑːn] is given as a Conamara word, which is a possible realisation of athadán. I don't actually know that much about the phonology of dialects outside Donegal, but this resource says intervocalic /h/ 'tends to disappear'.
